sections.h2: Coffee County housing at a glance
sections.html:
Coffee County is in south Georgia's Wiregrass region. The county seat and biggest town is Douglas, joined by Ambrose, Broxton and Nicholls. Land area comes to 575 of its 603 square miles.

In 2020 the census found 43,092 residents, 15,277 households and 17,331 housing units, of which 11.9% sat empty. Homeowners lived in 63.9% of occupied units and renters in 36.1%. If you are selling acreage, read the land programs below first, because farm or conservation enrollment changes what the buyer takes on.

Coffee County splits tax work between two neighboring offices. For values and appeals, go to the Tax Assessors Office, 224 West Ashley Street, Suite C, Douglas, weekdays 8:00 to 5:00, phone 912-384-2136. Personal property has a separate number, 912-493-1100.

Next door in Suite B, the Tax Commissioner takes care of bills, payments and homestead applications. Walk-in hours are 8:00 to 4:50 on weekdays, and the number is (912) 384-4895. Write to P.O. Box 1207, Douglas, GA 31533, or pay online through the commissioner's site. Anything about a bill belongs here, since the assessors deal only in values.

Cities add their own property tax, and some counties fold it into one bill. If your house is in Douglas, Broxton, Nicholls or Ambrose, ask the commissioner whether you will see one bill or two.

Mark April 1. Homestead filings, personal property returns and the conservation use, preferential and forest land programs all close then, although the land programs also accept applications during the appeal window. Your status is judged as of January 1, when you must own the home and be living in it.

Coffee County filing dates
Filing or programDeadline
Homestead exemptionJanuary 1 to April 1
Personal property returnApril 1
Conservation use, preferential and forest land applicationsApril 1, or during the appeal window

Parcels are also re-examined across a three-year cycle by contract appraisers from GMASS, who carry ID badges and drive marked vehicles. A recent sale within 12 months, a building permit, a value return, fire damage, a demolition or an appeal can bring a visit to your lot. Most of that fieldwork happens from January 1 through May 1, so a seller may meet an appraiser in spring.

Counting from the date printed on the assessment notice, you have 45 days. The county prefers real property owners to file through the appeals module on its qPublic site, and computers in the lobby let you do it in person. Personal property appeals go on paper, postmarked by the deadline if mailed.

Each appeal lands with the assessors first. Should they stand by the number, a Board of Equalization hears it next, and Superior Court remains open to an owner who is still unsatisfied. Arbitration is an alternative to the hearing. You can argue taxability, value, or uniformity with comparable properties. You cannot argue that the bill itself is too big.

No notice in the mail? Phone the assessors and check which address they have. The copy they hand you is treated as the official notice.

Homestead applications go to the Tax Commissioner's office, any time from New Year's Day to April 1 of the first year you want the break. Once approved, it continues each year until the owner changes. The county offers:

  • A standard homestead exemption.
  • A $4,000 exemption for owners 65 or older.
  • A school tax exemption for owners 62 or older under an income limit, capped at $10,000 of assessed value.
  • A $50,000 exemption for qualifying disabled former service members, extended to an unremarried surviving spouse or minor children.
  • A deferral for homestead owners 62 and older with gross income of $15,000 or less. Deferred tax is due when ownership changes or when the deferred amount plus interest reaches 85% of the property's fair market value.

Lawmakers can change these amounts, so check each one with the Tax Commissioner before counting on it. In a year when the Homeowners Tax Relief Grant is funded, expect to see it as a credit on your bill.

Landowners have extra choices. Qualifying farmland can be assessed at 30% of market value instead of the usual 40%. Conservation use requires a 10-year covenant and a $10.00 recording fee filed with the application. Breaking it costs twice the taxes saved, with 1% monthly interest added if the break is never reported. A buyer who keeps the land in the same use can sign onto the covenant.

December 20 is the default state due date, but a local government can move it. Some counties choose December 1, November 15 or installments. What matters is the date printed on your Coffee County bill, and the Tax Commissioner can confirm it. Interest waits until 60 days after the bill is postmarked, with penalties possible later.

If you paid tax that was assessed in error, a written refund request within three years can recover it. Refunds from appealed values come automatically after the value is final. A balance left unpaid can turn into a lien and a tax sale, which any closing office will insist you clear.

Tell your closing attorney if the land is enrolled in conservation use, because a buyer who changes how it is used can trigger the penalty.

sections.h2: Selling a Coffee County house: taxes at closing
sections.html:
The January 1 title holder is the one taxed, and how the year gets divided between you and the buyer is a matter for the contract and settlement statement. Your closing attorney should ask the Tax Commissioner, (912) 384-4895, for a payoff that includes any city bill. After closing, report the sale so your homestead exemption comes off, and remind the buyer to file theirs by April 1.

  • Get the balance as it stands today and find out about any city bill.
  • See whether the parcel sits in conservation use, which carries a covenant to the buyer.
  • Plan for dropping your homestead exemption.
  • Hold on to the closing statement. It proves the taxes were paid.
  • Bring a copy of your assessment notice and any appeal papers to the closing attorney.

Repairs you have put off, tenants in the house or back taxes can slow a conventional sale. A cash buyer skips the lender's appraisal, which leaves the payoff figure and the title work as the main things setting the closing date.

faqs.q: Who do I call in Coffee County with a tax question?
faqs.a: Call the Tax Commissioner, (912) 384-4895, about bills, payments and homestead filings. Call the Tax Assessors Office, 912-384-2136, about values and appeals. Because the assessors only set values, a bill question sent to them gets forwarded.

faqs.q: When is the Coffee County homestead filing deadline?
faqs.a: April 1 of the first year you want the exemption, and you must own and live in the home on January 1. File with the Tax Commissioner. An application that comes in later generally waits until the next tax year.

faqs.q: How long do I have to appeal a Coffee County value?
faqs.a: Forty-five days from the date on your assessment notice. Real property owners are steered to the qPublic appeals module, while personal property appeals go on paper.

faqs.q: Does Coffee County conservation use pass to a buyer?
faqs.a: It can. If the buyer keeps the same qualifying use and signs the covenant, there is no penalty. Changing the use within the 10-year period costs twice the taxes saved, so mention enrollment to your closing attorney.

faqs.q: How is the tax bill handled at a Coffee County closing?
faqs.a: The balance, including any city bill, is paid from your proceeds, and the contract sets each side's share of the year. Ask the Tax Commissioner for a payoff dated to your closing.
